structure.title: Economy · Counting the cost of a house
structure.text: Before we get the pond, we get the price of nails. Thoreau asks how many hours of a person's life shelter, clothing and food should cost. His detailed bills give a neighbour who disagrees with him something more definite to dispute than a declaration of independence.

structure.title: Where I Lived, and What I Lived For – Brute Neighbors · A working day at the pond
structure.text: Reading, hoeing beans, entertaining callers and going to the village occupy successive chapters. The railway can be heard at the cabin. Distance from Concord keeps changing with the visitor, the errand and the claims a locomotive whistle makes on the imagination.

structure.title: House-Warming – Conclusion · Ice, soundings and thaw
structure.text: Winter brings fishermen and commercial ice cutters, then spring brings minute changes in the banks beside the railway. Months at one address allow the same patch of water to appear as a measurement problem, a commodity, a neighbourhood and a living calendar.

people.name: Henry David Thoreau
people.text: The voice that offers an exact recipe for bread may shortly make an outrageous claim about the life of an entire town. Thoreau invites a neighbourly kind of disagreement. One can check his figures, question his preferences or walk down to look for oneself.

people.name: The railroad
people.role: A frequent caller at the pond
people.text: Its whistle measures part of Thoreau's day as reliably as a birdcall. Trains bring the wider commercial world within earshot of a man trying to decide what he can do without. He can admire the engine and question the terms of its journey.

context.title: Two years arranged as one seasonal round
context.text: Thoreau lived at the pond for over two years. The book gathers recurring activities and seasons into a shaped account. A chapter on sounds or on visitors collects observations he could never have made in the course of a single afternoon.

notice.text: See what he leaves out of a calculation.
notice.why: His account of the cabin makes a case about labour as much as cash. Borrowing an axe or working on land another person owns makes a difference to what a second builder could accomplish for the same price.

notice.text: Stay with a measurement after the number is found.
notice.why: Sounding the pond answers local stories about its bottomless depth. Thoreau's pleasure in finding a depth does surprisingly little to diminish his sense of wonder at what he has measured.

opening: Thoreau builds a small house near a pond and begins keeping accounts. He wants to know how much life the ordinary necessities actually cost, and how many supposedly necessary expenses merely purchase more work. His experiment leaves time for beans, visitors, ice, birds, and thoughts that a busier arrangement might never permit. The book can be funny, exacting, and infuriatingly confident, but its provocation is concrete: examine what occupies your days closely enough to discover whether you would choose the bargain again.
